The heat exchanger geometry consists of a single tube with a length of 200mm and a shell diameter of 20mm.
The geometry is simplified to account for planar symmetry and is cut in half vertically.
The k-omega turbulence model had lower RMS residual levels, around 1e-06, compared to the k-epsilon model, which had residual levels around 1e-03.
The k-omega model had a higher total heat transfer rate at the outlet of the inner tube compared to the k-epsilon model.
The inlet boundary conditions include a velocity of 0.01 m/s and temperature of 30°C for the inner tube, and a velocity of 0.05 m/s and temperature of 25°C for the outer tube.
The outlet boundary conditions are pressure outlets with a backflow total temperature of 26.85°C.
The solid components, such as the tube and shell, were modeled using aluminum and copper materials.
The temperature contours showed a more uniform temperature distribution in the k-omega model compared to the k-epsilon model.
The study concluded that the k-omega model is best suited for the heat exchanger analysis, as it provided better heat transfer rates and a tighter numerical convergence.
Heat exchangers have a wide range of applications, including in the food and beverage, petroleum, hydrocarbon processing, pharmaceutical, automotive, and power industries.
The three main heat transfer mechanisms discussed are conduction, convection, and radiation, with conduction and convection being the most common in manufacturing industries.

The overall heat transfer coefficient is defined by the equation: 1/U = 1/h_h + 1/h_c + Δx/k + R_f, where h_h and h_c are the hot and cold side heat transfer coefficients, Δx/k is the wall resistance, and R_f is the fouling resistance.
The logarithmic mean temperature difference (LMTD) is used to estimate the average temperature difference across the heat exchanger, and a higher LMTD will result in a smaller heat transfer area.
The energy balance equations for the hot and cold fluids are: Q = m_h C_p,h (T_h,i - T_h,o) and Q = m_c C_p,c (T_c,o - T_c,i).
The Navier-Stokes equations and the energy equation are the governing equations solved in the CFD analysis.
